doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Growing up among writers in a bookish family
summary: Collier says he was surrounded by commercial writers who were always broke, and explains the New England reading tradition that filled his childhood home with books.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Did you have a sense that you were going to be a writer even before you went to Hamilton?

No. I was surrounded by writers growing up. And I mean I knew people like Malcolm Cowley, I knew Matthew Josephson, I never really knew Cummings but I’ve met him, but the writers I basically knew were people like my father and my uncle and various others, who were commercial writers. And they were always broke. My idea of a writer was a man in a bathrobe weeping limp, telling the man from the finance company that the check was in the mail. I mean that was my idea of what a writer was. But nonetheless it was a very bookish family. This is the important thing. Not that we were terribly literary. My uncle did have ambitions to write novels and he did write a very good one eventually. But my father was basically concerned with seeing if he could make a living freelancing, which he really couldn’t. So it was not so much that we were literary in that sense but we were very bookish going way back. If you look at the history of this you understand that the Massachusetts Bay Colony, which was far more important than the Plymouth people we hear so much about, the Bay Colony, they knew what they were doing, they knew how to make the thing work, they came over on a bunch of ships, they came over with oxen and plows and everything they needed but they were intellectual avante garde and a great many of them had come from Cambridge University in England and they had come over as an intellectual adventure as well as to build Golden Hill in the Golden City on the Hill in the wilderness and that sort of thing. They were interested in this intellectual side of it. And what they understood was that each person had to decide for himself precisely what God intended, and that meant you had to know The Bible. So that meant that everybody had to be able to read. There was more literacy in Massachusetts in the 1630s than there is in the United States today. These people could all read. And that tradition carried down through New England and that was the tradition I grew up in, a very bookish tradition. The people in my family who had money, and there were not very many of them, but the ones I knew who were able to live without working, they read —

there was just a routine of several hours a day reading. And if the weather were bad and you didn’t have company to see or something, you might read all day long. Or if somebody were knitting and somebody else would be reading to them. You know it was just sort of books everywhere. And the great house that I was familiar with as a kid, my own family had no money, we were broke the whole time, but in my great aunt’s house there were just books everywhere. And in the house I grew up in there were books everywhere. And people today in the current generation with the electronic media would find it very difficult to understand that in my family the five of us, my brother, my sister, myself and my parents, after dinner would all be sitting in the living room reading. And I don’t mean we were all reading Trollope or Dickens or something, although my mother had three sets of Trollope and read Trollope endlessly. We might be reading The Saturday Evening Post. But we were reading.

Instead of watching. So by the time — I was reading adult books by the time I was nine simply because they’d be lying there somewhere and I’d pick it up and start reading it. I was reading Rebelais when I was in high school, I was reading Dickens when I was in high school, just because the sets of the stuff were there. You wanted something to read, oh I think I’ll read Oliver Twist.
